note: The seat of nerve and of collapse. Kannada puts courage here, not in the heart — ಕೆಚ್ಚೆದೆ, a chest of embers — and puts the loss of courage here too.

kids.note: Said of watching someone you raised do well. Not self-pride — pride on behalf of another, which English needs a whole clause for.
The same event one degree louder, and slightly comic if you use it about yourself.
The standard word for dismay. Kannada names the physical drop and leaves the feeling to be inferred — it does this constantly.
Reserved for news that arrives all at once. English 'heartbreak' has drifted toward romance; this has not.
Onomatopoeic, and specifically anticipatory — the fear of a thing you can see coming.
A single event, not a state. There is no English noun for the one jolt.
ಕೆಚ್ಚು is heat held in the body. The bravery word in Kannada is thermal, not moral.
The willingness to stand up and say it. Closer to 'having the guts' than to 'courage', and located one organ higher.
The state just before tears, named as a load rather than a mood.
ಸಂಕಟ is used equally for a dying person's distress, a moral dilemma, and unbearable news. The body and the ethics share a word.

note: Appetite, envy and grudging. Kannada is unembarrassed about siting the ugly feelings in the stomach, and says them out loud.

kids.note: The everyday word. The literary ಅಸೂಯೆ and ಮಾತ್ಸರ್ಯ exist, and nobody says them at home.
Distinct from envy — this is the heat of having been wronged, not of wanting what another has.
Used far past food: a full belly is the standard image for having had sufficient of anything.
Satisfaction as cooling rather than filling — the other half of how Kannada thinks about want.
Moral disgust and physical nausea in one phrase, with no metaphor marker between them.
The disgust that makes people renounce things, rather than merely push a plate away.
An insult about appetite that transfers cleanly to money and power.
ಆಸೆ is desire and is morally neutral; the prefix does all the work.

note: The most untranslatable seat. In Kannada the gut is the organ of kinship — your child is your ಕರುಳ ಬಳ್ಳಿ, your gut-vine — so every feeling sited here is about your own people.

kids.note: Involuntary, on seeing a child or an animal in distress. Pity is a judgement; this is a reflex, and Kannada marks the difference.
The considered version of the same movement — what you do after the gut has stung.
The image is wringing a wet cloth. Used for watching suffering you cannot stop.
Older and softer than ಕನಿಕರ, and slightly literary now.

kids.en: the grief of losing your own
kids.note: Kept for the death of a child or parent. Using it lightly would be shocking.
Names the swell, not the weeping — the moment before it breaks.
The umbilical cord as a creeper. English has no everyday phrase that says kinship is physical.
Flows one way only: parent to child, elder to younger, teacher to student. English 'love' has no direction; this word is nothing but direction.

note: The general seat, and the only one that is not an organ you could point to. Everything that can be said of a body here can be said of the mind — it fills, shrinks, lightens, opens.

kids.note: ನೋವು is bodily and emotional pain with no distinction at all. This is simply the ordinary way to say someone hurt you.
Specifically between two people who were close. Not anger, not grief — the cooled-off residue that keeps them apart.
What Kannada said before ಖಿನ್ನತೆ was coined. The older phrase is a description; the new word is a diagnosis.
One word for bored, mildly sad, and fed up. 'ಬೇಸರಾಗಿದೆ' could be any of the three and the listener reads your face.
The nearest Kannada gets to the therapeutic sense of 'vulnerable' — and note it is an act you perform, not a state you are in.
The permission to tease someone, eat off their plate, drop the honorific. Intimacy defined as permission rather than as feeling.
Said of a song, a gesture, a line of poetry. The agent is the thing, not you.
Both the feeling and its expression — to ಮೆಚ್ಚು someone silently is slightly incomplete.
Specifically after confessing or weeping. Relief as a change in weight.
Sharply distinct from ಶಾಂತಿ, peace as the absence of conflict. You can have ಶಾಂತಿ in a house with no ನೆಮ್ಮದಿ in it.
Distinguished from agreeing out loud. You can say yes without your ಮನಸ್ಸು having agreed, and Kannada gives you the phrase to say so.
Both the comfort someone gives you and the state it produces. Its negation, ಅಸಮಾಧಾನ, is the standard word for resentment.

note: Worry and dignity. The head overheats, spoils and spins — and it is also the thing you raise or lower in front of other people.

kids.note: Worry as a thermal problem. You can tell someone not to take ತಲೆಬಿಸಿ the way you would tell them to cool down.
ಚಿಂತೆ is also simply 'thought'. To worry and to think are the same word, which tells you something.
Same verb as milk going off. Used for exam season and for genuine breakdown, with the seriousness carried by tone.
Confusion as too many voices at once — the word is also used for an actual noisy crowd.
Physical dizziness and 'I can't take any more' share the phrase entirely.
A sound-word with no parts that mean anything on their own — the flap of not knowing what to do with your hands.
Self-respect described entirely as a posture held in public. ಘನತೆ is the abstract noun, this is the thing people actually say.
Shame as the same axis in the other direction. Kannada's shame is social and visible before it is internal.

note: The surface. Everything here is involuntary and visible — the hair standing up, the burn, the forgetting of the body altogether.

kids.note: Specifically aesthetic. You would say it about a raga or a line, rarely about good news.
Classical poetics counts it as visible evidence of an inner state, which is why it has its own noun.
Which of the two it is comes from context alone. Kannada declines to separate the physiology.
The Sanskrit register of exactly the same event.
The point at which anger stops being an opinion. Also literally a fever or a rash — the phrase does not choose.
Not an episode but a temperament, and one you wear on your face.
The highest praise available for listening to music. Also what you say about someone who missed their stop.
The grammar is the point: ಪರವಶ means under another's control. The feeling is driving.

note: The public instrument. These are the feelings other people read off you, whether or not you meant them to — which is why the sulk lives here and not in ಕೋಪ.

kids.note: Sulking described as a thing you actively do to your own face. The performance is the point.
The anger you are only entitled to with someone who loves you. It wants soothing, not resolution, and would be insulted by an apology that was merely correct.
The visible fall when someone hears they were left out.
ಸಪ್ಪೆ is what you call unsalted food. A dejected face is described as under-seasoned.
Reversible in a way English is not: a sight can also ಕಣ್ಣು ತುಂಬು you — fill your eyes by being beautiful.
Plain compound, no ceremony. Kannada saves its ceremony for the phrases around it.
A warning read by everyone in the room. The threat is in the description, not in any word for anger.
The literary register — ರೌದ್ರ rasa's everyday cousin.
The gesture that covers modesty, shyness and guilt without distinguishing them.
A bride's ನಾಚಿಕೆ and a thief's are the same noun. English needs three words and grades them differently; Kannada trusts context completely.
